lines.text: An ancient Red Sea coast, an Italian colony, a thirty-year war and a hard-won freedom. This is the story of Eritrea.
In the highlands, the town of Qohaito flourished for more than a thousand years, through the age of Aksum.
On the coast, Adulis became the Red Sea port through which Aksum traded with the wider world.
Aksum itself, a kingdom of coins and carved obelisks, spread across these highlands and turned to Christianity in the fourth century.
Later, on the high plateau, Asmara took root, the city that would become the capital.
In the late nineteenth century Italy began a mountain railway from the port of Massawa up to Asmara.
Eritrea became Italy's first colony, and Asmara was rebuilt in the modernist style, until Britain took over in 1941.
In 1938 Asmara gained a filling station shaped like an aeroplane, the Fiat Tagliero building.
In 1946 Isaias Afwerki was born. He would lead the liberation front, and then the country.
Joined to Ethiopia after the war, Eritreans took up arms in 1961. Their fight for independence would last thirty years.
In 1993 Eritreans voted, and almost all of them chose independence.
Eritrea was free at last, a new nation on the Red Sea, with Isaias as its president.
Only five years later, a border war with Ethiopia broke out, and afterwards Eritrea became one of the most closed states on Earth.
Born in 2000, the cyclist Biniam Girmay would make history in 2024, the first black African to win a stage of the Tour de France.
From the port of Adulis to a nation that fought for its name, Eritrea's story is one of endurance.
